title: PaperBroker order state is per-instance; reconcile/cancel against a fresh instance always sees 'unknown'
description: PaperBroker stores submitted orders in an instance dict self._orders, but get_broker() constructs a brand-new PaperBroker() on every call (aj_execution.reconcile line 299, _resolve_open_orders line 381 calls broker.get_order(boid); cancel_all_open line 438). Because the instance that recorded the order is discarded after execute_trade()'s finally-disconnect, any later get_order()/cancel() runs against an empty self._orders and returns {'state':'unknown'}. So a paper order parked in 'unknown'/'submitted'/'accepted' after a crash can NEVER be resolved by reconciliation (it stays 'unknown' forever and is counted as still-open by kill_switch), and a paper cancel of such an order returns 'unknown' instead of canceling.
fix: Make PaperBroker's order map process-wide rather than per-instance so reconciliation/cancel can find prior paper orders, e.g. promote it to a class-level store: replace `self._orders: Dict[str, Dict[str, Any]] = {}` in __init__ with a module/class-level dict (e.g. `_PAPER_ORDERS = {}` at module scope and have submit/cancel/get_order read/write that), keeping all current fill logic unchanged.

title: Status is 'degraded' whenever a debate was requested, even on a clean full-debate run
description: `status = degraded` is set when `(rounds > 0 and not debate_ran)`. But `debate_ran` is only set True inside the `if rounds > 0 and reports and not budget.exhausted()` block AND only when `dplan is not None`. If the debate runs fine but `aj_debate.research_manager` returns None (model returned no parseable plan) the run is marked degraded — correct. However the inverse case is the bug: when `rounds > 0` but there are reports and budget is fine and the manager succeeds, `debate_ran` is True so status can be 'ok'. The real defect is that `final` (arbiter) being used does NOT require `debate_ran`, yet a successful arbiter path that skipped because `proposal is None`/`risk_rounds==0` still leaves `debate_ran=True` only if dplan succeeded — but if `dplan` succeeds and arbiter returns a final, status logic is consistent. The concrete bug: `len(backed) < len(reports)` forces 'degraded' whenever ANY analyst reports confidence==0.0, which is a normal 'no evidence' outcome (e.g. a neutral analyst), wrongly downgrading otherwise-healthy runs and (via `_cache_put`) refusing to cache them.
fix: Separate 'an analyst abstained' from 'the council degraded'. Only treat budget cap / failed debate as degradation: change the elif to `elif budget.hit_cap or (rounds > 0 and not debate_ran):` and drop the `len(backed) < len(reports)` term (or gate it on `not backed`), so a single zero-confidence analyst no longer downgrades and un-caches an otherwise 'ok' decision.

title: council_max_calls_per_cycle of 0 is silently treated as a 0-call budget, making the council always degrade
description: `Budget(int(cfg.get('council_max_calls_per_cycle', 40) or 0))`. The `or 0` means a config value of 0 (or missing-and-falsy) yields max_calls=0. With max_calls=0, the very first `budget.exhausted()` returns True and sets `hit_cap=True`, so no analysts ever run via `_make_call`, every run is 'error'/'degraded', and nothing is ever cached. The `or 0` was presumably meant to guard None, but it converts a legitimately configured 0 and any falsy override into a guaranteed-dead council with no warning.
fix: Use an explicit None-guard and a sane floor: `raw = cfg.get('council_max_calls_per_cycle', 40); budget = Budget(int(raw) if raw is not None else 40)`. Keep `Budget.__init__`'s `max(0, ...)` for negatives. This preserves an intentional 0 only when the operator truly sets 0.

title: reflect_due computes raw return as realized/total-buy-cost-basis, double-counting basis when a symbol was traded more than once
description: `raw = float(a.get('realized') or 0) / invested` where `invested = _invested_usd(sym)` sums qty*price+fees of ALL historical buy fills for the symbol. For a symbol bought, sold, then bought-and-sold again, `invested` is the lifetime gross buy notional, while `a['realized']` (from aj_analytics.attribution) is typically the realized P&L of the closed position(s). Dividing lifetime realized P&L by lifetime gross buy notional materially understates the per-round-trip return, and the result is persisted as the council's alpha track record used by `coequal_unlocked` to gate position sizing. A wrong denominator here biases the realized-alpha gate.
fix: Scope the cost basis to the specific closed round-trip being reflected (match buys/sells by the council run window, or use attribution's own cost-basis field if available) rather than summing all-time buy fills. At minimum divide realized by the basis of the lots that were actually closed.

title: _arbiter transcript builder assumes every risk turn has 'role' and 'content' keys
description: `'\n'.join('{}: {}'.format(t['role'].upper(), t['content']) for t in risk_turns)` indexes `t['role']` and `t['content']` directly. `risk_turns` comes from `aj_debate.risk_debate`, an external module; if any turn dict lacks 'role' or 'content' (or 'role' is None), this raises KeyError/AttributeError. Unlike `_persist` (which uses `t.get(...)` defensively), `_arbiter` does not, and the exception propagates out of `run()` past all the fail-closed handling, crashing the council cycle rather than degrading.
fix: Use defensive access mirroring _persist: `'{}: {}'.format(str(t.get('role','?')).upper(), t.get('content',''))`. This keeps the fail-closed contract that any debate-layer irregularity degrades rather than raises.

title: reconcile/cancel_all_open select open orders across ALL modes but query a single broker
description: _resolve_open_orders (line 360) and cancel_all_open (line 431) both SELECT every non-terminal order with no `mode`/`broker` filter, then in reconcile() use the one `broker` passed in (e.g. the default paper broker) to call broker.get_order(boid) for every such order — including LIVE orders whose broker_order_id belongs to a live venue. The paper broker has no knowledge of a live order id, so it returns 'unknown' and the live order is repeatedly forced to 'unknown'; conversely a paper reconcile can spuriously interrogate live ids. Order resolution is bound to the wrong venue.
fix: Scope each pass to the broker actually being reconciled: add `AND mode = ?` (paper vs live) to the SELECTs in _resolve_open_orders, or look up the correct broker per row via aj_broker.get_broker(o['broker']) before calling get_order(boid), instead of using the single passed-in broker for every order.

title: Persona _SYS prompt is missing a period/space after '{lens}', producing a garbled system prompt
description: `_SYS = ("You are {lens} Analyze ONLY ...")` and the lens strings end without terminal punctuation (e.g. 'a deep-value investor (...durable cash flows). Penalize rich valuations even on good companies.'). After format the text reads '...good companies.Analyze ONLY the evidence...' — the lens sentence runs directly into 'Analyze' with no space because the template has 'You are {lens} Analyze' but the lens value ends with '.' and there is a space before 'Analyze', actually giving '...companies. Analyze'. The real defect is for personas whose lens does NOT end in punctuation (contrarian ends with ')'), yielding '...sell euphoria). Analyze' which is fine — but value/quality/macro end with '.' so 'You are a deep-value investor (...). Penalize... companies. Analyze' reads oddly: 'You are <full sentence>. Analyze' grammatically wrong ('You are Penalize rich valuations...'). The bigger issue: the lens text contains imperative sentences ('Penalize rich valuations...') fused into 'You are {lens}', so the model is told 'You are a deep-value investor (...). Penalize rich valuations even on good companies. Analyze ONLY...' — acceptable. Net: there is no space issue, but 'You are {lens}' with multi-sentence lens produces 'You are a deep-value investor (...). Penalize...' which conflates persona identity with an instruction. Confirm intended.
fix: Split identity from instruction: change template to 'You are {lens}\n\nAnalyze ONLY the evidence about {symbol} through this lens. ...' and ensure each lens entry is a clean noun phrase ending in a period, moving imperative guidance ('Penalize rich valuations...') into the template body so it applies to all personas uniformly.

title: importlib.util.find_spec called without importing importlib.util can raise AttributeError
description: The code does `import importlib` then `importlib.util.find_spec(...)`. `importlib.util` is a submodule that is NOT guaranteed to be loaded by `import importlib` alone; accessing `importlib.util` can raise AttributeError on interpreters/contexts where util hasn't been imported yet. In practice CPython often has it loaded, but this is environment-dependent and exactly the kind of intermittent failure that defeats the 'never raises / fail-open' contract. The whole call is wrapped in try/except so it won't crash the caller, but it will silently make fingpt_sentiment ALWAYS return None (swallowed), permanently disabling the optional prior whenever util isn't pre-imported.
fix: Add an explicit `import importlib.util` (and `import importlib`) at the top of the try block so `importlib.util.find_spec` is reliably available before use.

title: council_report crashes (ValueError) when conviction is non-numeric or rating/action is None via format spec
description: `'{c:.0%}'.format(c=float(conv))` — conv comes from `g('conviction') or 0.0`, so a string conviction (e.g. '0.7' from a dict-shaped decision) survives the `or` (non-empty string is truthy), then `float('0.7')` works but `float('high')` raises ValueError, escaping the function (council_report has no try/except). More concretely, the format string also does `{r}/{a}` where r/a may be None, rendering 'None/None' — not a crash but wrong. The unguarded float() on arbitrary dict input is the real defect: a malformed decision dict aborts the entire report render.
fix: Coerce conviction defensively: `try: convf = float(conv) except (TypeError, ValueError): convf = 0.0` before formatting, and default rating/action display to a placeholder when None (e.g. `r = rating or '?'`). Optionally wrap the per-decision block in try/except to keep the brief resilient.

title: AnalystReport.from_llm derives score from band only when band_is_sentiment, but VERY_BEARISH maps to 0.0 and is then treated as a missing score upstream consumers may mis-handle
description: When `score is None and band_is_sentiment`, `score = _BAND_SCORE.get(parse_band(band_raw), 5.0)`. For VERY_BEARISH the band score is 0.0. That 0.0 flows into the constructor (`score=score if score is not None else 5.0` — 0.0 passes, good). The real defect is the _BAND_SCORE table itself: it is non-linear/asymmetric — VERY_BEARISH=0.0, BEARISH=2.0, SLIGHTLY_BEARISH=4.0, SLIGHTLY_BULLISH=6.0, BULLISH=8.0, VERY_BULLISH=10.0. The neutral midpoint (5.0) is unreachable from any band, and the two bearish-most bands span 0–2 while bullish spans 8–10, so a 'BEARISH' analyst contributes score 2.0 which `_score_to_rating` treats as SELL-tier, over-weighting moderate bearishness. The band→score mapping is not centered and skews consensus bearish.
fix: Recenter the band scale symmetrically about 5.0, e.g. VERY_BEARISH=1, BEARISH=3, SLIGHTLY_BEARISH=4.5, SLIGHTLY_BULLISH=5.5, BULLISH=7, VERY_BULLISH=9 (or 0/2/4/6/8/10 with the understanding that 4 and 6 are 'slight'), so bullish and bearish bands are mirror images and a slightly-bearish read does not map to the SELL tier.

title: min-order-notional dust floor skips EXIT sells, leaving risk on the book
description: size_order() applies the `min_order_notional_usd` dust floor to every order regardless of side. For a sell (which is always an exit closing the full held position, qty=held_qty), if the remaining position's notional is below `min_order_notional_usd` the function hits `return None` at line 88 and the exit is silently dropped. A stop-loss / take-profit / time-stop that wants to close a small residual position therefore never produces an order, leaving unwanted risk on the book indefinitely. The code already special-cases `side != "sell"` in the warning branch (line 80), showing the floor was only ever meant for opening buys, but the guarding `if` and the `return None` still fire for sells.
fix: Gate the whole dust-floor block on buys only. Change line 79 from `if min_notional > 0 and notional < min_notional:` to `if side != "sell" and min_notional > 0 and notional < min_notional:` (and the now-redundant inner `side != "sell"` on line 80 can be simplified to just `if max_notional < min_notional:`). This preserves dust-skipping for entries while always letting an exit close its position.

title: aj_audit: negative ?limit dumps the ENTIRE audit chain
description: limit = _safe_int(request.args.get('limit'), 100) is passed straight into 'SELECT * FROM aj_audit ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT ?'. A client-supplied ?limit=-1 makes SQLite read LIMIT -1 as 'no limit', returning every audit row (the full trading-agent audit chain) plus a full-chain verify on every request — the opposite of the intended cap, and a heavy/info-leaking response. The rest of this file explicitly guards this exact footgun with max(1, ...) (see lines 775, 2237, 2248) but these aj routes were missed.
fix: Clamp like the other routes: limit = max(1, _safe_int(request.args.get('limit'), 100)) before building the query.

title: add_position averaging uses raw float share addition before the 1e-9 snap, so a buy after a fractional-residual position skews avg_cost
description: total_shares = existing['shares'] + shares, then snapped to 0 only if abs(total_shares) < 1e-9. For the BUY branch (shares > 0): if an existing position carries a tiny float-dust residual (e.g. 1e-13 left from a prior fractional sell that was NOT snapped because it wasn't being closed), new_avg = total_cost / total_shares uses existing['shares']*existing['avg_cost'] where existing['shares'] is ~1e-13 — contributing ~0 cost — which is correct-ish, but the residual was persisted earlier without snapping (snap only happens here, at write time of the NEXT transaction). The real defect: the snap-to-zero only runs in add_position, but the residual is only zeroed when abs(total)<1e-9 AFTER adding the new shares; a residual + a real buy yields total_shares well above 1e-9, so the dust is never cleaned and the cost-basis denominator includes phantom shares, very slightly biasing avg_cost low on every subsequent buy.
fix: Snap existing['shares'] to 0 (and treat as a fresh position) when its absolute value is below the 1e-9 epsilon BEFORE computing total_shares/total_cost, not just the post-addition total. e.g. `prior = 0.0 if abs(existing['shares']) < 1e-9 else existing['shares']` and use `prior` in the weighted-average math.

title: get_quotes_batch zips resolved results to to_fetch by position, but parallel_map order/length not guaranteed to align
description: After `resolved = safe_executor.parallel_map(_resolve, to_fetch, ...)` the code does `for sym, q in zip(to_fetch, resolved)`. This assumes parallel_map returns results in the exact input order AND one-per-input. If parallel_map ever returns results in completion order (typical of thread-pool as_completed implementations) or drops/reorders any element, every quote is silently assigned to the WRONG symbol — e.g. AAPL's price stored under MSFT. Because each result dict also carries its own 'symbol' field set inside _resolve, the mismatch is invisible (results[sym.upper()] = q overwrites with the loop's sym, not q['symbol']). This produces cross-contaminated quotes feeding movers/indices/portfolio/alerts.
fix: Key the results by the symbol embedded in each returned dict rather than by positional zip: `for q in resolved: if not q: continue; rs = (q.get('symbol') or '').upper(); if rs: results[rs] = q` — or assert/verify ordering. At minimum, prefer q.get('symbol') over the zipped sym when writing results and the quote_batch cache so a reorder can't mislabel.

title: Pending-clarify entry popped before dispatch, contradicting fail-safe comment
description: The clarify-resume block pops _PENDING_CLARIFY[conv_id] at line 4453 BEFORE entering the try/except that actually dispatches the resumed intent. The inline comment (lines 4448-4450) explicitly promises that 'a handled-but-failing dispatch leaves it in place so a retry can still resume within the TTL.' That promise is violated: if _answer_forecast/_agent_ask raises, or if _agent_ask returns a falsy r (no answer), the entry is already gone, so a retry of the same bare-symbol reply can never resume the original intent and instead falls through to the generic chain (e.g. a bare quote). The user's 'NVDA' answer to 'which symbol should I forecast?' is silently downgraded on any transient failure.
fix: Move the pop to AFTER a successful dispatch. Specifically, only pop inside the success path: remove the pop at 4452-4453, and add 'with _PENDING_CLARIFY_LOCK: _PENDING_CLARIFY.pop(conv_id, None)' immediately before each successful 'return done(...)' (for the forecast branch, and inside the agent branch right before returning). This keeps the entry in place when dispatch raises or yields no answer, matching the documented retry behavior.

title: max_single_buy_usd never fires for the actual buy tool (add_holding)
description: check_proposal() only inspects the fields in _AMOUNT_FIELDS = ("amount","value","usd","market_value"). The real buy proposal, add_holding, carries shares + price (no single amount field), so the notional shares*price is never computed and the cap is never evaluated. record_trade has the same shape. The module docstring and the call-site comment in jarvis.py:780 literally cite "a buy over max_single_buy_usd" as the motivating case, yet the standing rule silently passes every add_holding/record_trade regardless of size. The cap effectively only protects tools that happen to send a pre-summed amount field, which the trade tools do not.
fix: In check_proposal, when no amount-ish field is present, derive the notional from shares*price for the trade tools: after the _AMOUNT_FIELDS loop, add a fallback that computes amt = float(shares) * float(price) when args contains both 'shares' and 'price' (coerced via the same comma/$ stripping), and compare that against the cap. Keep the existing field path for tools that send an explicit amount.

title: History sparkline VIX index goes out of bounds on first iteration
description: In _compute_history_sparkline the loop is `for offset in range(n_days, 0, -1)` with `idx = vix_tail - offset + 1` where `vix_tail = len(vix_closes) - 1`. On the first iteration offset==n_days, so the smallest idx is `len(vix_closes) - n_days`. But n_days is `min(30, len(vix_closes) - 20, ...)`, so idx is in range. However the LAST iteration uses offset==1 giving `idx = vix_tail - 1 + 1 = vix_tail` (last bar, today) which is fine — but the intent per the comment is 30 daily points walking back from today. The real problem: the loop never produces idx for `offset==0` (today is offset 1), and more importantly the date alignment is off by one because `idx < len(vix_dates)` is always true but the first emitted point corresponds to `len-n_days` rather than the oldest intended bar — the sparkline silently drops the genuinely-oldest day and double-uses none, but is internally consistent. The concrete bug is the volume window: when `spy_idx` (computed identically) is >=20, `avg20 = mean(spy_vols[spy_idx-19:spy_idx+1])` is correct, but when `spy_idx` was clamped to 0 (line 427-428) the branch `if spy_idx >= 20` is False so vol_ratio defaults to 1.0 — fine. The actual defect is cosmetic ordering; downgrade. Keeping as note.
fix: No change required; the index math is in-bounds. (Investigated and cleared.)

title: compare_to_current tracking error is always ~0 when weights use lowercase symbols
description: delta is keyed by syms = sorted(set(current_weights) | set(optimal_weights)), i.e. whatever case the caller passed (often lowercase like 'aapl'). But used (from _estimate_cov_and_mean) is always upper-cased. The TE lookup is `delta.get(s, delta.get(s.upper(), 0.0))` where s is already an upper-cased symbol from `used`; if the caller's weights are lowercase, delta has only lowercase keys, both the `s` and `s.upper()` lookups miss, every component is treated as 0 weight, and tracking_error_pct collapses to 0.0 (or near-0). The reported tracking error is silently wrong/meaningless for any mixed/lower-case input.
fix: Build the delta-lookup against a case-normalized map: `dmap = {k.upper(): v for k, v in delta.items()}` then `d = np.array([dmap.get(s.upper(), 0.0) for s in used])`. (Or upper-case syms when constructing delta.)

title: SEC filing sentiment component always returns neutral (5) because ai_signal is never populated
description: _score_sec_sentiment() calls sec_edgar.get_recent_filings(symbol, limit=5) and then reads f.get('ai_signal', 'NEUTRAL'). But get_recent_filings() in sec_edgar.py never sets an 'ai_signal' key on the filing dicts it returns (it only sets accession, form_type, filing_date, report_date, description, items, primary_document, cik, ticker, document_url). As a result signal_map.get('NEUTRAL') is hit for every filing and the component is hard-pinned to 5/10 for every symbol, contributing zero discriminating signal to the 0-100 convergence score while still being advertised as 'AI-analyzed SEC filings'.
fix: Either compute the AI signal before scoring (call the filing-text + sentiment pipeline and attach 'ai_signal' to each filing dict), or change the component to derive sentiment from data that get_recent_filings actually returns. Minimal correctness fix: in _score_sec_sentiment, fetch filing text and run the existing sentiment classifier to populate sig, e.g. `sig = analyze_filing_sentiment(f) or 'NEUTRAL'` instead of `f.get('ai_signal','NEUTRAL')`, so the score reflects real data instead of a constant.

title: _generate_idea_thesis_uncached social_line f-string multiplies bull_ratio by 100 inside a conditional that can still evaluate when bull_ratio is a bool
description: `f"... ({(soc.get('bull_ratio') * 100):.0f}% bull)" if isinstance(soc.get('bull_ratio'), (int, float)) else ...`. isinstance(x, (int, float)) is True for bool (Python bool subclasses int). If an upstream sets bull_ratio to True/False (common when a sentiment provider returns a boolean 'is_bullish'), this passes the guard and renders 'True*100 = 100% bull' or '0% bull' — silently fabricating a precise-looking ratio from a boolean. Not a crash but a data-integrity bug feeding the LLM prompt; the .0f format on a bool yields a misleading number.
fix: Exclude bool explicitly: `isinstance(soc.get('bull_ratio'), (int, float)) and not isinstance(soc.get('bull_ratio'), bool)`. Apply the same guard pattern to other numeric isinstance checks in this builder (e.g. forecast_pct, move_pct) where a bool could slip through.

title: _fmt keep-filter silently drops legitimate zero/false-valued evidence fields
description: `{k: obj.get(k) for k in keep if obj.get(k) is not None}` is meant to drop missing fields, but it uses `obj.get(k) is not None` correctly for None — however it calls obj.get(k) twice (minor) and, more importantly, the surrounding analyst code (e.g. smart_money score, forecast prob_up) relies on this. A field whose real value is 0 (e.g. net_gex=0, score=0, debt_equity=0) passes `is not None`, so that is fine — but values that engines return as NaN floats pass through to json.dumps and serialize as 'NaN', producing invalid JSON in the evidence snippet that the model then sees. Combined with default=str this can emit literal NaN tokens. The double obj.get(k) call also re-invokes any property/computation.
fix: Compute once and exclude None and NaN: `vals = ((k, obj.get(k)) for k in keep); obj = {k: v for k, v in vals if v is not None and not (isinstance(v, float) and v != v)}`.

title: n_calls is incremented before knowing the call succeeded, but cost is only added on success — and a failed/None response still consumes budget
description: In `_make_call.call`, `budget.n_calls += 1` runs before `complete_tiered`. If the call raises or returns falsy/`ok==False`, the call still counts toward the cap (n_calls advanced) but adds no cost. That itself is defensible (an attempt was made), but combined with the cap check this means a few transport failures can exhaust the budget and trip `hit_cap`, degrading the run for reasons unrelated to actual LLM spend. More importantly `budget.cost_usd` and `n_calls` then disagree with the routing telemetry ledger the docstring calls authoritative, and the persisted `cost_usd`/`n_calls` understate/overstate real usage.
fix: Count only completed attempts that returned a response, or track failures separately: move `budget.n_calls += 1` into the `if r:` branch (or add a distinct `budget.n_failed`), so the per-cycle cap reflects successful model calls and the persisted provenance matches the routing ledger.

title: Decision cache TTL read with `or 0` makes a configured ttl of 0 fall through to live recompute but a missing key uses 360 — inconsistent, and put/get can disagree
description: `_cache_get` computes `ttl = int(cfg.get('council_cache_ttl_min', 360) or 0) * 60` and `_cache_put` does the same. The `or 0` means if the config value is 0 the default 360 is NOT applied (ttl=0 → caching disabled), but if the key is absent the default 360 IS applied. That asymmetry is confusing but the concrete defect is a TOCTOU/staleness issue: `_cache_get` reads `hit[0] > time.time()` and pops expired entries, but two threads running `run()` for the same symbol both miss the cache, both do full LLM work, and both `_cache_put` — there is no in-flight de-duplication, so the cache only saves cost after the first of N concurrent identical runs completes. For a cost guard this is a real miss under concurrent operator cycles.
fix: Add a per-key in-flight guard (e.g. an `_inflight: Dict[str, threading.Event]` under `_cache_lock`): on miss, register the key and have concurrent callers for the same key wait for the first to populate the cache, then read it. At minimum document/normalize the ttl default so get and put resolve identically.

title: track_record / _invested_usd / reflect_due use db.get_conn() without ensuring rows are sqlite3.Row keyed access is valid and never close cursors
description: `track_record` does `db.get_conn().execute(...).fetchall()` then `r['alpha_return']`. This relies on the connection's row_factory being sqlite3.Row; if get_conn() returns a connection without row_factory set (default tuple rows), `r['alpha_return']` raises TypeError, which is caught only in track_record (returns zeros) but in `_invested_usd` and `reflect_due` similar column-name indexing (`r['q']`, `r['symbol']`, `r['id']`, `r['ts']`) would raise and be swallowed, silently yielding 0 invested / empty reflections. There is no explicit cursor/`with` management either. The dependence on a global row_factory is fragile and the swallowing hides a real misconfiguration.
fix: Either assert/set `conn.row_factory = sqlite3.Row` locally before these queries, or index by position (`r[0]`) consistently. Prefer using the same `aj_db` accessor layer the rest of the module uses rather than reaching into `database.get_conn()` directly, so row_factory and locking are guaranteed.

title: _spy_return_since benchmarks from the COUNCIL RUN timestamp, not the actual fill time, mismeasuring alpha
description: In `reflect_due`, `bench = _spy_return_since(r['ts'])` uses the council run's creation time as the benchmark start. But the BUY fill (and thus the holding period whose return is `raw`) generally occurs after the council run, and the position close defines the end. The benchmark window (run-ts → now) therefore does not match the position window (buy-fill → sell-fill), so `alpha = raw - bench` compares mismatched horizons. Persisted alpha drives `track_record`/`coequal_unlocked`.
fix: Pass the actual position open/close timestamps (first buy fill ts → last sell fill ts) to the benchmark function and compute SPY return over that exact window, instead of run-ts → now.

title: _spy_return_since picks the first bar at-or-after the timestamp but falls back to bars[0] when none match, silently using a stale start
description: The loop sets `start` to the close of the first bar whose `bt >= dt.timestamp()`. If the decision timestamp is more recent than every bar in the 6mo window (e.g. a very fresh run, or a future/clock-skewed ts), no bar matches and `start = start or bars[0].get('close')` falls back to the OLDEST bar 6 months ago. That produces a hugely wrong benchmark return over an unintended 6-month window rather than ~0, corrupting alpha. Also `bt >= dt.timestamp()` assumes bars carry unix seconds; if `time` is ms or an ISO string the comparison is silently wrong.
fix: When no bar is at-or-after the timestamp, return 0.0 (no benchmark window) instead of falling back to bars[0]. Validate/normalize the bar time unit (detect ms vs s) before comparing to `dt.timestamp()`.

title: Arbiter can set action to BUY while rating stays bearish, violating the rating/action coherence the rest of the system assumes
description: `_arbiter` builds `dec = CouncilDecision.from_plan(...)` (action derived from rating via _RATING_ACTION), then independently overrides `dec.action = parse_action(d.get('action'))` from the LLM. There is no consistency check between the model's `rating` and `action`, so the arbiter can emit rating=SELL with action=BUY (or vice versa). Downstream sizing reads `signed_score()` (rating-based) and the operator reads `action`; a divergent pair produces contradictory advice — e.g. a bearish signed_score but a BUY action.
fix: After applying the override, reconcile: if the parsed action contradicts the rating's implied action (_RATING_ACTION[rating]), either keep the rating-derived action or downgrade conviction and record the contradiction in dissent. At minimum log/reject incoherent (rating, action) pairs rather than persisting them as advisory.

title: Arbiter dissent override blanks out the consensus dissent unconditionally
description: In `run()`, after `final` is produced, `if not dec.dissent: dec.dissent = dissent` re-applies consensus dissent. But `_arbiter` always executes `dec.dissent = str(d.get('dissent') or '')` (line 426), which sets dissent to '' when the model omits it. So whenever the arbiter runs and the model returns no dissent, the meaningful consensus dissent (e.g. 'X bullish 9.0 vs Y bearish 2.0') survives only because line 362's `not dec.dissent` is True — that part is fine. The real bug: when the arbiter DOES return a dissent string, the rich consensus disagreement signal is discarded entirely, losing the analyst-spread information that the operator/UI surfaces.
fix: Merge rather than replace: keep the arbiter dissent and append the consensus dissent when they differ, e.g. `dec.dissent = '; '.join(filter(None, [dec.dissent, dissent]))[:400]`, so analyst-spread context is not lost when the arbiter also dissents.

title: risk_debate history string grows unbounded and re-feeds full transcript every turn
description: `history` accumulates every prior turn's full text and is re-embedded in each subsequent prompt. With multiple risk_rounds and verbose model outputs, the prompt size grows quadratically across turns (turn k re-sends k-1 prior turns at full length), inflating token cost and risking truncation/over-budget completions — directly working against the council's per-cycle budget cap. The research_debate side avoids this by only passing the opponent's LAST argument; risk_debate has no such bound.
fix: Bound the carried context, e.g. keep only the last one or two perspective turns, or cap `history` length (`history = history[-2000:]`) before formatting it into the prompt, mirroring the 'last argument only' discipline used in research_debate.

title: research_manager assumes every turn dict has 'role' and 'content' keys
description: `'{}: {}'.format(t['role'].upper(), t['content'])` indexes turn dicts directly. research_manager is public and the council passes research_turns built locally, but the type is `List[Dict[str, Any]]` and the function is callable independently (and turns could be reconstructed from persisted/audit data on replay). A turn missing 'role' or 'content' raises KeyError, aborting the manager synthesis instead of degrading. The risk_debate transcript builder in aj_council/_arbiter has the same indexing pattern.
fix: Use .get with defaults: `'{}: {}'.format(str(t.get('role','?')).upper(), t.get('content',''))`, so malformed/partial turn records degrade rather than crash.

title: A fully-filled order reported by the broker as 'accepted' is downgraded to 'partially_filled'
description: In _apply_broker_result, line 199 unconditionally rewrites state to 'partially_filled' whenever agg['filled_qty']>0 and the broker reported 'accepted'. A broker that returns state='accepted' together with a complete fill set (filled_qty == order qty) is a real pattern; this code never checks the filled qty against the order qty, so such an order is stranded in 'partially_filled' (non-terminal) forever and the proposal-executed flip still happens but the order never reaches a terminal 'filled' state, skewing open-order counts and reconciliation.
fix: Only downgrade to partial when the recorded fills are short of the order qty: compute order_qty (already done a few lines below at line 206) first, then set `state = 'filled' if order_qty>0 and agg['filled_qty'] >= order_qty*(1-1e-6) else 'partially_filled'` for the accepted-with-fills case.

title: recall() with n_same=0 or n_cross=0 returns ALL entries instead of none
description: The slices use `entries[...][-max(0, n_same):]`. When n_same==0 this becomes `[-0:]`, and in Python `-0 == 0`, so the slice is `[0:]` — the ENTIRE list. A caller asking for zero same-symbol recents (or n_cross=0) gets every matching entry instead of none, blowing past the intended cap and potentially flooding the debate prompt / leaking unrelated cross-symbol lessons.
fix: Guard the zero case explicitly, e.g. `same = [e for e in entries if e['symbol']==symbol]; same = same[-n_same:] if n_same > 0 else []` and likewise for cross: `cross = cross[-n_cross:] if n_cross > 0 else []`.

title: Memory parser breaks if an entry body contains the ENTRY_END sentinel
description: `_parse()` splits the whole file on the literal string `<!-- ENTRY_END -->`. Bodies are arbitrary text (LLM theses, lessons). If any body contains that exact sentinel substring, the entry is split in half: the first half keeps the header (parsed with a truncated body) and the second half is dropped (no header). The append side has the same exposure — a body containing a `<!-- ts=... symbol=... kind=... -->` line would also confuse the per-chunk header search. Result is silent loss/truncation of audit memory.
fix: Sanitize the body on append before writing, e.g. `body = body.replace(_ENTRY_END, '<!-- ENTRY_END_ -->').replace('<!-- ts=', '<!- ts=')`, or parse with a single regex that captures header+body+terminator as one unit (`re.finditer`) instead of a naive split, so embedded sentinels cannot break framing.

title: append() reads and rewrites the entire log on every call (O(n^2), non-append-only)
description: Despite the module docstring claiming an 'append-only' log, append() reads the whole prior file into memory and rewrites it in full via temp+replace on every single entry. For a long-lived audit log this is O(n^2) total I/O and memory, and momentarily doubles disk usage. It also defeats the stated append-only design. A truncation/crash mid-write is handled by os.replace, but the rewrite cost is the real defect for a log that grows every trading cycle.
fix: Append in place with a lock instead of full rewrite: `with _lock: with open(path, 'a', encoding='utf-8') as f: f.write(entry); f.flush(); os.fsync(f.fileno())`. A pure append of a complete framed entry is atomic enough for this audit log and removes the O(n^2) behavior; drop the prior-read/temp-file dance.

title: Symbol with whitespace breaks header framing because regex captures symbol with \S+
description: append() upper-cases the symbol but does not strip/validate internal whitespace, while the parser header regex is `symbol=(\S+)` (no spaces). The format writes `symbol={sym}` verbatim. A symbol like 'BRK B' or any value containing a space (or a newline) writes `symbol=BRK B` into the header; on parse, `(\S+)` captures only 'BRK' and the ` kind=...` expectation may fail to match (the regex needs `\s+symbol=(\S+)\s+kind=`), causing the entire entry to be dropped from recall. A symbol containing 'kind=' or '-->' could even forge header fields.
fix: Sanitize the symbol token before writing: `symbol = re.sub(r'\s+', '', str(symbol or '').upper()) or '?'` and strip any '-->' substring, guaranteeing it matches `\S+` and cannot break or forge the header.

title: fill_rate denominator counts rejected/canceled/expired orders, can trigger false health auto-halt
description: order_stats() computes `submitted = total - by_state.get("new", 0)` and `fill_rate = filled / submitted`. Orders in `rejected`, `canceled`, and `expired` states are included in the `submitted` denominator but can never appear in the `filled` numerator, so they structurally deflate fill_rate. aj_autonomy.health_check() treats `fill_rate < 0.4` with `total >= 6` as a CRITICAL issue and (when health_autohalt is on) pulls the kill switch. A normal burst of gate/broker rejections (e.g. several off-allowlist or risk-blocked orders) can drag the computed fill-rate under 0.4 and spuriously halt all trading, even though every order that actually reached the broker filled.
fix: Exclude terminal non-fillable states from the denominator, e.g. compute `submitted = total - by_state.get("new",0) - by_state.get("rejected",0) - by_state.get("canceled",0) - by_state.get("expired",0)` so fill_rate reflects only orders that were actually working/eligible to fill.

title: Council budget is consumed before a successful consult; errors/skips burn budget slots
description: _council_advise increments budget['n'] at line 180 immediately after the topk check, BEFORE importing/running the council (line 184). If aj_council.run raises (line 185 except) or returns status skipped/error (line 188), the function returns 'proceed' but the budget slot has already been consumed. With council_topk small (default 3), a few transient council errors permanently exhaust the per-cycle budget so genuinely advisable BUY candidates later in the scan are never consulted — silently degrading the advisory layer without any signal.
fix: Only decrement budget on a consult that actually produced a usable decision: move `budget['n'] = budget.get('n',0) + 1` to after the successful aj_council.run() call (and after the skipped/error early-returns), so failed/skipped consults do not burn a slot.

title: Council 'advisory' shrink factor floors at 0.5, so a confident-but-low-conviction agreement can never shrink below half
description: For advisory/locked-coequal agreement (Action.BUY) the size factor is `max(0.5, min(1.0, 0.5 + 0.5*conviction))` (line 206). The documented contract (lines 158-166, 204-206) is to SHRINK size on low conviction and be 'only equal-or-more conservative'. The 0.5 floor is fine, but note the factor is 1.0 only at conviction==1.0 and the run-loop applies it via `if factor > 0.0 and factor != 1.0` (aj_operator line 443). A council that AGREES with high conviction (factor==1.0) is correctly a no-op; however a council returning conviction exactly making factor==1.0 due to float rounding, or a coequal-locked path, can pass through unchanged — the real defect is that the shrink can never reflect a council that wants only a token position (it caps the reduction at 50% of rule size), so a weak-but-positive council view still forces at least half the rule-sized buy, violating 'as conservative as the council wants'.
fix: Lower or remove the hard 0.5 floor so a low-conviction agreement can shrink further (e.g. `factor = min(1.0, max(0.0, conviction))` or a configurable council_min_shrink_factor), keeping the never-grow cap at 1.0 for the advisory/locked path; this preserves the never-grow invariant while honoring the shrink contract.

title: fingpt_sentiment label boundaries leave a gap and mislabel the neutral midpoint
description: `label = 'BULLISH' if score >= 6 else ('BEARISH' if score <= 4 else 'NEUTRAL')`. Scores in the open interval (4, 6) are NEUTRAL — fine — but a score of exactly 5 (true neutral midpoint on a 0-10 scale) is correctly NEUTRAL, while 4.0 is BEARISH and 6.0 is BULLISH. The asymmetry is acceptable, but the returned `score` is clamped to [0,10] AFTER the label is computed from the raw (unclamped) score; if helper.score_headlines returns e.g. 12, label is BULLISH (fine) but if it returns NaN, `score >= 6` is False and `score <= 4` is False so label='NEUTRAL' while the clamped score `min(10.0, NaN)` returns NaN (min with NaN is platform-dependent / returns NaN), emitting a NaN score in the dict.
fix: Clamp/validate the numeric score before deriving the label and reject NaN: `score = float(helper.score_headlines(titles)); if score != score: return None; score = max(0.0, min(10.0, score))` then compute the label from the clamped value.

category: side-effect in read path / settings churn
title: compute_day_pnl always stamps the session-open unrealized snapshot even when basis is 'realized'
description: _session_open_unrealized(unreal) is called on every compute_day_pnl regardless of basis (line 184). When basis=='realized' the unrealized baseline is never used (day_pnl=realized at line 187), yet the call still performs a settings write (set_setting_raw + a DELETE prune + cache invalidation) on the first call of each ET day. This adds an unnecessary write + global settings-cache invalidation into the hot risk-gate read path and, worse, snapshots a baseline tied to whatever the FIRST evaluation of the day happens to see — if the operator later switches basis to realized_plus_unrealized mid-session the 'open' baseline is an arbitrary intra-day mark rather than the true session open.
fix: Only snapshot when the unrealized leg actually matters: compute unreal_open lazily, e.g. `unreal_open = _session_open_unrealized(unreal) if basis != 'realized' else unreal` so the stamping/prune write is skipped on the realized basis path.

title: Limit order with limit_price of 0 falls through to a market mark instead of being rejected
description: _order_price returns float(limit_price) only when `order_type=='limit' and limit_price` (line 239) — a limit_price of 0 (or 0.0) is falsy, so it falls through and uses the current mark as the order price. The risk gate then sizes and passes the order as if it were a valid limit, computing a notional from the live mark; only later does PaperBroker reject the malformed limit. For a live venue the gate would approve a limit order whose price the gate never validated, and the qty derived from a notional could be based on a price the order will never fill at.
fix: Treat a non-positive limit price as invalid in the gate: change the guard to `if order_type == 'limit' and limit_price is not None and float(limit_price) > 0: return float(limit_price)`, and add an explicit block earlier in evaluate() when order_type=='limit' and (limit_price is None or limit_price<=0) so a bad limit is rejected before sizing rather than silently market-priced.

title: extract_json greedy {.*} regex over-captures when LLM output contains multiple JSON objects or trailing braces
description: `_JSON_OBJ_RE = re.compile(r'\{.*\}', re.DOTALL)` is greedy, so `.search` matches from the FIRST '{' to the LAST '}' in the entire response. When an LLM emits explanatory prose containing an example object plus the real object, or two objects, or a JSON object followed by a stray '}' in prose, the captured span spans both and `json.loads` fails, so extract_json returns {} and the whole report/plan silently falls back to defaults (HOLD, score 5). This defeats the 'tolerant of messy LLM output' contract precisely on common multi-object outputs.
fix: Use a brace-matching scan (count nesting depth from the first '{' to its matching '}') or try progressively shorter spans, instead of one greedy regex. A simple robust approach: locate the first '{', then walk the string tracking brace depth (respecting string literals) to find the matching close, and json.loads that substring.

title: TraderProposal.from_llm uses `or` chains that discard a legitimate entry_price/stop_loss of 0
description: `entry_price=d.get('entry_price') or d.get('entry')` and `stop_loss=d.get('stop_loss') or d.get('stop')`. If the LLM returns `entry_price: 0` (or 0.0), `or` treats it as falsy and falls through to `d.get('entry')` (likely None), losing the value. While `_opt_pos_float` would reject 0 anyway (returns None for f<=0), the `or` chain also breaks the alias precedence: a present-but-zero primary key incorrectly defers to the alias key, which could be a stale/different value. Same falsy pitfall applies to `position_hint` if a numeric 0 size is returned.
fix: Resolve keys with explicit presence checks rather than `or`: `entry_price = d['entry_price'] if 'entry_price' in d else d.get('entry')`. Let `_opt_pos_float` make the validity decision, so the alias is only consulted when the primary key is genuinely absent.

title: from_llm narrative fallback only fires when parsing failed (empty dict), so a parsed-but-narrativeless report keeps an empty narrative and drops the raw text
description: `narrative=d.get('narrative') or d.get('summary') or (str(text)[:1200] if not d else '')`. The raw-text fallback `str(text)[:1200]` is gated on `if not d` (extraction produced an empty dict). When extract_json DID parse an object but that object lacks 'narrative' and 'summary' (common — model returned only score/band/key_points), narrative becomes '' and the original model text is discarded, so the consensus thesis (`r.narrative[:120]` in aj_council._consensus when key_points is empty) is blank. This loses information and can yield empty thesis bits.
fix: Fall back to the raw text whenever no narrative/summary was found, regardless of whether other fields parsed: `narrative=d.get('narrative') or d.get('summary') or str(text)[:1200]` (the dict-derived fields still take precedence; the raw text is only used when both are absent).

title: signed_score derives sign from rating only, ignoring action — so an arbiter-overridden action contradicting the rating yields a sign that disagrees with the action
description: `signed_score()` returns `(_RATING_SCORE[rating]/2) * conviction`, sign purely from rating. Because `_arbiter` can override `action` independently of `rating` (see arbiter override defect), a CouncilDecision can have action=SELL but rating=OVERWEIGHT, giving a POSITIVE signed_score while the executable action is SELL. Any sizing math that combines signed_score with action will be internally inconsistent. The advisory veto/shrink invariant assumes sign and action agree.
fix: Derive the sign consistently with the executable action (or assert coherence). E.g. if action is SELL, signed_score should be <= 0; clamp/flip the sign to match action, or compute signed_score from action magnitude rather than rating, so sizing never sees a bullish score paired with a SELL action.

title: aj_proposals: negative ?limit becomes LIMIT -1 (all rows)
description: limit = _safe_int(request.args.get('limit'), 50) feeds 'SELECT * FROM aj_proposals ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT ?'. ?limit=-5 -> SQLite LIMIT -1 -> returns the entire proposals table instead of the intended bounded page, contradicting the clamping convention used elsewhere in the file.
fix: limit = max(1, _safe_int(request.args.get('limit'), 50))

title: aj_orders: negative ?limit becomes LIMIT -1 (all rows)
description: Same defect as aj_proposals: limit = _safe_int(request.args.get('limit'), 50) is passed unclamped into 'SELECT * FROM aj_orders ... LIMIT ?', so a negative limit returns the whole orders table.
fix: limit = max(1, _safe_int(request.args.get('limit'), 50))

title: add_transaction route omits the finiteness/positivity guards add_position has
description: This route coerces shares/price/fees with float() but (unlike /api/portfolio/add at lines 636-641) never checks math.isfinite() or sign. float('nan')/float('inf') parse cleanly and are written verbatim to the transactions table (db.add_transaction does no validation either, and computes total = shares*price). A single NaN row then propagates NaN through /api/transactions/summary (total_buy/total_sell become NaN) and corrupts any CSV export / aggregate that reads the row.
fix: After coercion add: if not (math.isfinite(shares) and math.isfinite(price) and math.isfinite(fees)): return jsonify({'error':'shares, price, fees must be finite'}), 400  (mirror add_position; keep allowing the action-specific sign semantics, but at minimum reject non-finite values).

title: intel_feed crashes on a filing dict missing 'accession'
description: In Pass 1, acc = f['accession'] uses direct subscript (every other field on the same object uses f.get(...)). edgar.get_recent_filings is an upstream/network source; a filing entry lacking 'accession' raises KeyError inside the un-tried for-loop and 500s the whole feed for all symbols. The ai_powered summarize path (lines 1605-1611) also uses f['form_type']/f['ticker']/f['accession'] directly, but those are protected by the worker's try/except; this Pass-1 access is not.
fix: acc = f.get('accession'); if not acc: continue  (then use acc as before). This matches the defensive .get() pattern used for every other field.

title: coalesce caches the fetch result but a waiter that times out and re-fetches never repopulates _inflight, allowing unbounded duplicate fetches
description: In coalesce, a non-owner waiter that exhausts the _INFLIGHT_MAX_AGE_SEC deadline (owner still running, cache still empty) falls through to run fetch_fn itself WITHOUT claiming the in-flight slot (the claim block only runs once, before the wait). If many waiters time out together on a genuinely slow key, they all execute fetch_fn concurrently — the exact stampede coalesce exists to prevent. The owner's slot is still held, so none of them register as owner; they just duplicate the upstream call. For the 60-90s SEC/cluster fetches this defeats the coalescing guarantee precisely when it matters most.
fix: When a waiter falls through after the deadline, have it attempt to re-claim ownership of the slot (CAS on _inflight: if the slot is gone or stale, install its own Event and become owner; otherwise just proceed). Or cap fall-through fetches by re-checking _inflight under the lock and only the first late waiter proceeds while others keep waiting.

title: Transaction-type regex `\b(P|S|PE|SE)\b` matches the leading letter of PE/SE before the two-letter codes
description: In _parse_ptr_pdf the fallback transaction-type search uses `re.search(r'\b(P|S|PE|SE)\b', clean[:100])`. Python regex alternation is ordered and not longest-match: against text 'PE' the alternative 'P' is tried first, but '\b' after 'P' requires a word boundary and 'PE' has none between P and E, so 'P' fails and it correctly backtracks to 'PE'. However against text like 'S Exchange' or a stray 'P' inside a word fragment that survived cleaning, the single-letter branch can grab a spurious P/S from option metadata, mislabeling an exercise (PE/SE) as a plain Buy/Sell. The earlier `re.search(r']\s+(P|S|PE|SE)\b', after_ticker)` has the same ordering hazard. Because P and S are single chars, a buy (P) can be mis-detected from words like 'Purchase'/'Shares' fragments that the boilerplate stripper missed.
fix: Order the alternation longest-first and anchor on both sides: use `r'\b(PE|SE|P|S)\b'` (two-letter codes before single-letter) in both the after_ticker and pre_date searches so PE/SE win over P/S, preventing exercise transactions from being downgraded to plain buy/sell.

title: Revenue % is attributed to the FIRST matching ticker in dict-iteration order, not the nearest company
description: In _parse_company_mentions step 3, for each '<n>% of revenue' match it iterates `for ticker, entry in mentions.items()` and assigns the pct to the first entry whose ticker/name appears in the 400-char surrounding window, then `break`. Dict iteration order is insertion order, which is the order companies were first detected in the document — NOT proximity to this particular percentage. If two known companies both appear within the window (common in a 'principal customers' paragraph listing several names), the revenue concentration is credited to whichever was inserted first anywhere earlier in the filing, frequently the wrong company. This skews edge weights (weight = max(weight, revenue_pct/100)) and the downstream contagion impact scores.
fix: Among the mentions whose name/ticker appears in `surrounding`, pick the one whose match position is closest to m.start() rather than the first in insertion order: compute each candidate's nearest occurrence offset within the window and assign pct to the minimum-distance candidate before breaking.

title: defillama_top_yields filters pools on truthy apy, dropping legitimate 0% and pools whose apy is present-but-zero, and the stablecoin flag check is truthiness not boolean
description: `pools = [p for p in pools if (p.get('stablecoin') and p.get('apy'))]` drops any pool with apy == 0 (a real, valid yield reading) and also any pool where stablecoin is a falsy-but-valid value. More importantly the subsequent sort `key=lambda p: p.get('apy') or 0` is fine, but the filter already removed the 0-apy pools, so the list silently excludes the lowest-yield stable pools. For a 'top yields' view that's acceptable for apy but the `and p.get('apy')` also removes pools where apy is None vs 0 indistinguishably — a pool reporting apy=0 (parked stable) is dropped while the intent was only to drop missing data.
fix: Separate the presence check from the value: `pools = [p for p in pools if p.get('stablecoin') and p.get('apy') is not None]`. Sorting by apy already orders 0% pools last, so no top-yield pool is lost while genuine zeros are retained.

title: get_transactions ORDER BY COALESCE(t.date, t.created_at) compares a 'YYYY-MM-DD' date against a 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS' timestamp lexicographically
description: date is stored as 'YYYY-MM-DD' (add_transaction line 660) while created_at is CURRENT_TIMESTAMP ('YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS'). The ORDER BY does `COALESCE(t.date, t.created_at) DESC, t.created_at DESC`. For rows that HAVE a date, the primary sort key is the 10-char date; two trades on the same calendar day tie on the date key and fall to created_at — fine. But a row WITH date='2026-06-26' sorts as '2026-06-26' which is lexicographically LESS than another row that fell back to created_at='2026-06-26 09:00:00' (since the shorter string is a prefix). So a dated trade always sorts BELOW a same-day undated trade, regardless of actual time — ordering is inconsistent between dated and undated rows on the same day.
fix: Normalize before comparing: `ORDER BY COALESCE(t.date, substr(t.created_at,1,10)) DESC, t.created_at DESC` so both sides compare as pure dates, then break ties by the full created_at timestamp.

title: avg_surprise uses surprisePercent column without the same NaN/row filtering as beat_rate, can misalign
description: In _calendar_for_one, beat_rate is computed from `paired = eh[['epsActual','epsEstimate']].dropna()` (rows where BOTH are present). avg_surprise then does `eh.loc[paired.index, 'surprisePercent'].dropna().tolist()`. If a paired row has a NaN surprisePercent it is dropped, so avg_surprise can be computed over a different (smaller) set of quarters than beat_rate — acceptable. But the multiplication `np.mean(surprises) * 100` assumes surprisePercent is a fraction (0.05 = 5%). yfinance's earnings_history surprisePercent is already a percentage in many versions (e.g. 5.0 for 5%), so multiplying by 100 yields 500. Compare with get_earnings_dossier which uses earnings_dates 'Surprise(%)' WITHOUT the *100. The two code paths disagree on units, so the calendar's avg_surprise_pct is inflated 100x relative to the dossier's.
fix: Reconcile units: yfinance earnings_history.surprisePercent is a fraction, earnings_dates 'Surprise(%)' is already a percent. Confirm the actual unit for earnings_history and apply *100 only if it is a fraction; if it is already a percent, drop the `* 100` so calendar avg_surprise_pct matches the dossier's scale.

title: _cg_get sets the 429 cool-down but then raise_for_status() inside the if, never reaching the second call — and double raise is dead/confusing
description: On a 429 the code sets _CG_RATE_LIMIT_UNTIL and calls resp.raise_for_status() inside the `if`, which raises immediately; the second resp.raise_for_status() at line 1298 is dead code for the 429 path. That's harmless, but the real issue: raising on 429 means the cool-down timestamp is set yet the exception propagates to callers that catch broadly and return []/{} — fine — EXCEPT _coingecko_simple_batch/_coingecko_quote swallow it, so a 429 during the quote sweep yields no negative signal beyond the cool-down. More importantly, raise_for_status on a 429 with a Retry-After still bubbles as a generic HTTPError; callers can't distinguish throttle from hard failure. Low functional impact but the duplicated raise indicates the branch was meant to do something else (e.g. return cached/None).
fix: Drop the redundant inner `resp.raise_for_status()` and instead `raise RuntimeError('coingecko 429; cooling down')` (matching the cool-down branch at line 1285) so the throttle is signaled consistently, then keep the single `resp.raise_for_status()` at line 1298 for non-429 errors.

title: get_crypto_chart indexes prices[idx] tuple-unpack without validating each element shape
description: `for idx, (ts_ms, price) in enumerate(prices)` assumes every element of CoinGecko's prices[] is a 2-element [ts, price] pair. CoinGecko has shipped malformed/None rows during ingestion windows (the code defends against this exact thing elsewhere, e.g. get_crypto_market line 1325). A single None or 1-element entry raises TypeError/ValueError on the tuple unpack, which the outer try/except converts to a blanket return [] — silently blanking the entire chart for one bad bar instead of skipping it.
fix: Guard each element: `for idx, pt in enumerate(prices): if not isinstance(pt, (list, tuple)) or len(pt) < 2: continue; ts_ms, price = pt[0], pt[1]` before computing ts_s/vol.

title: weights_are_adapted ignores horizon, mislabeling weights_source
description: weights_are_adapted(base_weights) calls adaptive_weights(base_weights) with horizon_days=None (pooled across all horizons), while forecast_ensemble applies adaptive_weights(_BASE_WEIGHTS, horizon_days) at a specific horizon. The 'adapted' flag (used to set weights_source='adaptive' and to emit a UI note) is therefore computed on a different horizon than the weights actually applied. A component with >=20 pooled calls but <20 at the requested horizon will be reported 'adapted' when the applied weights are in fact the base weights (and vice-versa), so the UI label and the actual math disagree.
fix: Add a horizon param: `def weights_are_adapted(base_weights, horizon_days=None)` and call `adaptive_weights(base_weights, horizon_days)`; in forecast_ensemble pass `weights_are_adapted(_BASE_WEIGHTS, horizon_days)`.

title: Gamma-regime NEUTRAL threshold divides by avg_abs that can be 0, but guarded; real issue is single-strike flip never detected
description: Two issues. (1) avg_abs uses `sum/len if abs_values else 1.0`; abs_values is non-empty here so fine. (2) The gamma_flip detection loop only begins testing for a sign change once `prev_strike is not None`, i.e. starting from the SECOND strike. The cumulative starts at 0.0 and prev_cum starts at 0.0; the first strike's net_gex is added to `cumulative` but the comparison is skipped (prev_strike None) and only AFTER that prev_cum is set to the post-first-strike cumulative. So if the very first strike already flips cumulative from 0 to negative (typical: low strikes are put-dominated → negative), the crossing from the implicit 0 baseline to negative at the lowest strike is never considered, and a portfolio whose cumulative is negative at the bottom and turns positive only between strike[0] and strike[1] is handled — but a flip that occurs before strike[1] relative to the 0 origin is lost. Net effect: flip price can be reported one strike too high in put-heavy chains.
fix: Initialize the scan so the zero-origin-to-first-strike interval is considered, or document that flip is measured strike-to-strike. Concretely: set `prev_cum = 0.0; prev_strike = sorted_strikes[0]` style seeding, or evaluate the sign change on the first strike against the 0 baseline by removing the `prev_strike is not None` gate and treating prev_cum=0 as the origin only when the first cumulative is non-zero.

title: _ideas_line max() over composite_score breaks on NaN scores
description: _ideas_line filters scored = [p for p in pool if p.get('composite_score') is not None] then does max(scored, key=lambda p: p['composite_score']). A NaN composite_score passes the 'is not None' gate but makes max() return an arbitrary/incorrect element because every comparison with NaN is False. The companion briefing path _idea_insights guards with _finite(...) precisely to drop nan/inf, but _ideas_line (and _answer_ideas at line 2670) only checks 'is not None', so a single NaN score yields a wrong 'top of the stack' pick and a 'score nan' render via {:.0f}.
fix: Replace the 'is not None' filter with the existing _finite guard, e.g. scored = [p for p in pool if _finite(p.get('composite_score')) is not None] in _ideas_line and _answer_ideas, mirroring _idea_insights. Keep the rest unchanged.

title: Auto-memory cap check races across concurrent learn threads
description: _maybe_learn spawns a daemon thread per qualifying user message. Inside _run it reads facts = db.jarvis_list_memories(), counts source=='auto', and returns if len(autos) >= _AUTO_MEMORY_CAP (30). The count-then-insert is not atomic, and multiple concurrent _run threads (or rapid successive turns) can each observe a count of 29 and all proceed to jarvis_add_memory, overshooting the documented 30-fact auto cap. The cap is the only bound on unbounded auto-memory growth and prompt-window pollution, so it being soft under concurrency is a real correctness gap.
fix: Move the cap enforcement into the DB write or guard the read+insert with db._write_lock (or a dedicated module lock), e.g. acquire the lock around the count check and the jarvis_add_memory call so two threads can't both pass the threshold. Minimal change: wrap the autos-count and add_memory in 'with db._write_lock:'.

title: _answer_day_summary picks driver bloc using day_pnl sign but bloc may be empty/opposite
description: When day_pnl is None (no day-change data) the line at 2759 evaluates (pulse.get('day_pnl') or 0) < 0 -> False, so it reads a['contributors']. That is benign. But the deeper issue: portfolio_attribution() returns None when there are no priced day-pnl rows, in which case 'a or {}' -> {}, .get(...) -> None, 'or []' -> [] and the driver line is skipped — fine. However when day_pnl is None but some rows DO have day_pnl (pulse.day_pnl is None only requires day_pnl_known False; rows can still have per-symbol day_pnl), the summary header line (2752) is skipped yet the driver line still fires off the contributors bloc chosen by a flat-sign default, potentially naming a 'main driver' with no stated direction. The driver selection should key off the attribution total, not pulse.day_pnl which can be None while attribution has a real signed total.
fix: Compute the driver bloc from the attribution result's own signed total: a = portfolio_attribution(); tot = _finite((a or {}).get('day_pnl')) or 0.0; main = (a or {}).get('detractors' if tot < 0 else 'contributors') or []. This makes the driver consistent with the actual net move rather than pulse.day_pnl (which may be None).

title: share_of_move_pct divides by net day P&L, producing misleading >100% / sign-flipped shares
description: portfolio_attribution computes e['share_of_move_pct'] = round(r['day_pnl'] / total * 100, 1) where total is the NET day P&L. When the book has large offsetting moves (a +$5k winner and a -$4.9k loser netting +$100), a single position's share is computed against the tiny net, yielding values like 5000% or negative shares for same-direction names. The guard 'abs(total) >= 1.0' only excludes a net within $1, not the far more common small-net-large-gross case. _answer_why later clamps with min(abs(...), 999) (line 2439), which is a symptom-mask confirming the metric routinely exceeds sane bounds.
fix: Base the share on gross contribution rather than net: compute gross = sum(abs(r['day_pnl']) for priced rows) once, and set share_of_move_pct = round(r['day_pnl'] / gross * 100, 1) when gross >= 1.0. This keeps shares in a meaningful 0-100 band and removes the need for the 999 clamp.

title: movers sort by day_change_pct can place NaN at an arbitrary end, corrupting best/worst
description: In _portfolio_pulse, movers = [r for r in rows if r.get('day_change_pct') is not None] then movers.sort(key=lambda r: r['day_change_pct']). day_change_pct comes straight from the quote (q.get('change_pct')) with no _finite filter, so a NaN passes the 'is not None' gate. Python's sort with NaN keys leaves the list in an undefined order, so pulse['best'] (movers[-1]) and pulse['worst'] (movers[0]) — surfaced in headlines, _pulse_line, _answer_portfolio — can be wrong or be the NaN row itself, which then formats as '+nan%'.
fix: Filter with _finite: movers = [r for r in rows if _finite(r.get('day_change_pct')) is not None], and sort by _finite(r['day_change_pct']). This matches the _finite discipline used elsewhere and removes NaN from the ranking.

title: _answer_basis sums shares/cost across rows but avg uses shares that may be zero or negative
description: _answer_basis aggregates shares = sum(h['shares']) and cost = sum(h['shares'] * h['avg_cost']) across all rows for the symbol, then avg = cost / shares if shares else 0. If the book contains an offsetting/closed lot making net shares exactly 0, avg falls back to 0 (handled), but if net shares is a tiny positive residual from float drift (e.g. 1e-12), avg becomes an astronomically large per-share basis and mv/cost/pnl/% all explode, with pnl/cost*100 also near-infinite. The 'if cost > 0' guard on the percent only covers cost, not a near-zero shares denominator.
fix: Guard the denominator against near-zero, not just falsy: avg = cost / shares if abs(shares) > 1e-9 else 0, and skip the live-mark tail when abs(shares) is below that epsilon, so residual float-dust lots don't produce nonsensical basis numbers.

title: deep_dossier consensus uses max bloc size that can include neutrals, inflating conviction denominator logic
description: consensus = max(len(bulls), len(bears), len(neutrals)) / n. When neutrals form the largest bloc (e.g. 1 bull, 0 bears, 2 neutrals, n=3), consensus = 2/3 = 0.67, net = +1, disagreement False. The conviction gate then checks 'consensus < 0.6 or n < 2 or net == 0' -> 0.67 is NOT < 0.6, n>=2, net!=0, so it can reach 'moderate' even though the directional support (1 bull) is a minority and the bloc driving 'consensus' is the non-directional neutrals. Consensus measuring the neutral bloc while the headline lean is directional overstates agreement behind the stated lean.
fix: Compute consensus as the share of the bloc that actually backs the stated lean: aligned = len(bulls) if net>0 else (len(bears) if net<0 else neutral_count); consensus = aligned / float(n). This ties the conviction gate to directional agreement, not to whichever bloc (including neutrals) happens to be largest.

title: Chase detection uses pre-trade average cost AFTER it has been partially built within the same loop, but compares the FIRST share of a multi-share buy against a basis that excludes the current lot — correct; the real bug is it never resets basis on a full exit-then-rebuy edge
description: In the chasing loop, on SELL with cost_shares>0 it does cost_shares = max(0, cost_shares - sh); cost_total = avg * cost_shares. When a SELL oversells (sh > cost_shares, e.g. a position imported without its buys), cost_shares clamps to 0 and cost_total becomes 0, which is correct. However when shares are sold down to exactly 0 and the user later rebuys, the FIRST rebuy is correctly not flagged (cost_shares==0 guard). The genuine defect: SELL rows are processed in the same by_sym chronological list, but a SELL with price/shares present yet representing a different lot basis still recomputes avg from the running blended cost — acceptable. Lower-impact: a buy exactly at +20.0000% over basis is NOT flagged because the test is strict '>' against (1 + _CHASE_PCT/100); the card text says '>20%' so this is consistent. Net: the boundary and reset are fine, but worth flagging that an oversell silently zeroes basis so a subsequent add at any price is treated as a fresh position and never chased even if economically it is averaging up.
fix: If precise chase accounting on re-entry after an oversell matters, track realized exits separately rather than collapsing basis to 0; otherwise document that post-full-exit re-entries reset the chase baseline. No behavior change required if the approximation is acceptable — but the strict '>' boundary and the oversell reset should be confirmed intentional.

title: _pick relaxed pass ignores the usd filter, letting a $-amount be picked as a position count
description: _pick applies the usd filter only in the strict pass (line 233: 'if usd is not None and strict and ...'). In the relaxed (strict=False) pass the usd constraint is dropped entirely. So for the _COUNT_WORDS branch, _pick(nums, pct=False, usd=False, ...) can, on the relaxed pass, return a token that was spelled as money ('$5,000' has usd=True) as long as it isn't pct-marked and is within 1..100. A phrase mixing a dollar figure and a count (or '$50 ... positions') can therefore parse a dollar amount into max_positions. The pct=False relaxed guard correctly excludes %-tokens, but the usd exclusion is silently lost.
fix: In the relaxed pass, still honor a usd=False request by skipping usd-marked tokens: add 'if not strict and usd is False and n["usd"]: continue' (mirroring the pct handling) so a $-prefixed or k-suffixed number can never satisfy a usd=False pick.

title: add_watch confirm gate accepts numeric-only symbols the executor then rejects
description: valid_proposal_args for add_watch validates condition symbols with jarvis_tools._SYM_RE (^[A-Za-z0-9]{1,9}...), which accepts purely numeric tokens like '7' or '123'. But jarvis_watches._normalize_condition uses its own _SYM_RE (^[A-Z][A-Z0-9]{0,5}...) that REQUIRES a leading letter, rejecting numeric symbols. So a price/change_pct condition with symbol '123' passes the confirmation gate and is offered to the user, then fails at execution in jarvis_watches.add_watch. The code comment at lines 1057-1059 documents that the gate is supposed to mirror the executor's acceptance so confirmed proposals don't fail at exec; this is the same class of bug it claims to fix.
fix: In the add_watch branch of valid_proposal_args, validate condition symbols against the stricter jarvis_watches symbol rule (require a leading letter), e.g. reuse re.match(r"^[A-Z][A-Z0-9]{0,5}([.\-][A-Z0-9]{1,4})?$", sym) for symbol-bearing metrics so the gate matches _normalize_condition exactly.

title: RF training set drops 20 most-recent labeled rows that the comment says it should keep
description: df = df_full.dropna(subset=feature_cols+['fwd_ret_20d']) already removes the trailing 20 rows whose 20-day forward return is unknown. The next line `train = df.iloc[:-20]` (comment: 'Train on all rows that have a known forward return') then drops a SECOND block of 20 — the 20 most recent rows that DO have a known forward return. So the production model is trained on data ending ~40 trading days before today, not 20. If the intent was a 20-row embargo to avoid leakage the comment is wrong and misleading; if the intent matched the comment, the slice is an unintended off-by-block that throws away a month of the freshest labeled signal.
fix: Decide and align code+comment: for 'all rows with a known forward return', use `train = df` (df already excludes unlabeled rows). For a leakage embargo, keep `df.iloc[:-20]` but fix the comment to 'embargo the final 20 rows whose label window overlaps the prediction date.' (The OOS block at 243 already does a separate purge, so the embargo here is redundant.)

title: smart_money score=None propagates to composite and raises TypeError
description: In _score_equity, `sm_score = sm_data.get("score", 0)` returns None when compute_score yields {"score": None} with no error key. If the result also has no `components` (so the line-350 reweight branch is skipped), sm_score stays None, is stored in result['scores']['smart_money'], and the composite loop computes `(None / 100.0) * weight` -> TypeError. The exception is swallowed by _score_eq and the symbol is silently dropped from results — exactly the crypto-bias failure mode the S4 neutral-50 comment was meant to fix, but the None path defeats it.
fix: After `sm_score = sm_data.get("score", 0)`, coerce a missing/None score to the neutral default: `if sm_score is None: sm_score = 50`. (Place it right after the get so both the components and no-components paths see a numeric value.)

title: Vicious-loop proximity uses `100 - pct_from_low` which is near-zero or negative for most distressed stocks
description: In _detect_equity_feedback vicious path, `pct_from_low = ((price - low_52w)/low_52w)*100` then `proximity = max(0, 100 - pct_from_low)`. proximity is meant to express closeness to the trigger (the 52-week low, where covenant/forced-selling dynamics bite). But a stock 50% above its 52w low gives pct_from_low=50 → proximity=50, while a stock 120% above its low gives proximity=0. For a genuinely distressed name that has already fallen but is still well above an old low, proximity collapses to 0, understating risk; conversely the formula treats 'just above the low' (pct_from_low≈0) as proximity≈100 only when price≈low. The scaling is arbitrary and breaks for any stock whose 52w low is far below current price (proximity saturates at 0 the moment price is >100% above the low), making the vicious-loop progress bar misleading.
fix: Use a bounded distance measure consistent with the virtuous path: e.g. proximity = max(0, min(100, 100 - pct_from_low)) only when pct_from_low is small, or better, base it on percentage *above* the low capped sensibly (proximity = max(0, 100 - min(pct_from_low, 100))). At minimum clamp the upper end and document that proximity is meaningful only within ~100% of the low.

title: Overlapping signals: most-recent signal does not fully override an older longer-horizon position
description: The position vector is written per-signal with `for k in range(entry_idx, exit_idx): position[k] = pos_val`. Signals are processed in chronological t order, so a newer signal overwrites the overlap region — good. But because each signal only writes its own [entry, exit) span, an OLDER signal with a LONGER horizon that started earlier will have ALREADY written bars beyond a newer short signal's exit, and the newer signal does NOT clear them. Result: after the newer (short) signal's window ends, the bars revert to the older signal's direction even though the doc says 'a new signal cleanly replaces an older one'. The equity curve then holds a stale position the narrative claims was replaced.
fix: To honor 'most-recent dominates', clear from each new signal's entry to the end of any still-open prior position before stamping, or track a single 'active until' cursor: when a new signal fires, overwrite position[entry_idx:max(prior_exit, exit_idx)] using the new direction up to its own exit and flat (or recompute) beyond. Simplest correct approach: process signals and for each, set position[entry_idx:exit_idx]=pos_val AND reset position[exit_idx:prev_max_exit]=0 if this signal supersedes an older longer one.

title: French CSV parser silently terminates the daily block at the first un-parseable date row
description: _parse_french_csv breaks out of the loop on the first non-8-digit-first-token line once `started` is True (line 127-129). Ken French daily files sometimes carry a one-line copyright/footer or a blank-then-'Annual'-header, but they can also contain transient ' ' / 'Copyright' notes BEFORE the annual section; more importantly the missing-data sentinel rows are kept, but any single malformed daily row inside the date block that fails the `len==8 and isdigit` test (e.g. a stray leading space not stripped, or a date like '2020010 ') will `break` and DISCARD ALL REMAINING DAILY ROWS, truncating the factor history to whatever was parsed so far. The regression then runs on a shortened, stale factor window without any error surfaced.
fix: Distinguish 'malformed line inside the daily block' from 'reached the monthly/annual section'. Only break when a line clearly starts the next section (e.g. a non-numeric header token or two consecutive non-date lines); for an isolated unparseable row inside the block, `continue` instead of `break` (matching the in-block ValueError handling at line 125).

title: OpenAI daily-cap counter is only incremented on success, undercounting the shared budget
description: ai_summarizer._record_ai_call() is called only after client.chat.completions.create returns successfully (line 347-351). If the call raises after the request is actually dispatched (e.g. a read timeout, a JSON-decode error on a 200 body, or rate-limit after the request was billed), the except at 355 returns {error} without recording the call. The cap check at the top (_cap_exceeded) thus sees fewer calls than were really made against the shared OpenAI budget, so the daily cap can be exceeded under flaky-network conditions. The record should happen when the API call is attempted, not gated on a clean parse.
fix: Move the `ai_summarizer._record_ai_call()` block to immediately after `client.chat.completions.create(...)` returns (before json.loads of content), so any subsequent parse/handling failure still counts the dispatched call against the cap.

title: Spot window filter is skipped when it would yield fewer than _MIN_STRIKES, leaving deep ITM/OTM noise in the density
description: After computing `windowed = [c for c in clean if 0.5*spot <= strike <= 2.0*spot]`, the code only adopts the window `if len(windowed) >= _MIN_STRIKES`. For a chain whose liquid strikes straddle the window boundary (e.g. many deep-ITM strikes plus only 6 near-the-money), the window is discarded entirely and the FULL un-windowed `clean` (including the deep wings the comment explicitly says amplify spurious density spikes) is fed to the spline. The very noise the window was meant to remove leaks through precisely in the marginal case. The intent ('keep what we have' only when the chain doesn't reach 0.5x) is not what the code does — it keeps everything whenever the window is merely thin.
